content: The safety data for tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) during pregnancy is limited but suggests an excellent safety profile. However, TAF has not yet been approved for the prevention of mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of hepatitis B virus (HBV). Maternal Safety: A meta-analysis of six studies estimated an 8% risk of maternal HBV flare after discontinuation of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), which is statistically comparable to the 6% flare rate observed in untreated women. There is limited data on restarting antiviral therapy after postpartum flares. Infant Safety: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) evaluated the effect of TDF prophylaxis compared to placebo on infant bone mineral density. No statistically significant differences were observed in lumbar spine bone mineral density at one year of age. Breastfeeding is not contraindicated for women taking TDF, as the drug is present in very low concentrations in breast milk and has shown no evidence of toxicity in infants exposed through breastfeeding. The FDA classifies TDF as a Pregnancy Category B drug, indicating no adequate evidence of risk in humans, while entecavir (ETV) is classified as Category C. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 131 studies globally found that 21% of HBsAg-positive pregnant women had HBV DNA levels ≥200,000 IU/mL, with regional variations ranging from 8% in the Eastern Mediterranean to 31% in the Western Pacific. The pooled global estimate of HBeAg-positive pregnant women was 24%, with similar regional variations. Among HBsAg-positive pregnant women, 21% had high HBV DNA levels and were HBeAg-positive, while 76% had HBV DNA <200,000 IU/mL and were HBeAg-negative. The certainty of evidence was rated as moderate. WHO Recommendations: Since 2020, the World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended TDF prophylaxis for HBsAg-positive pregnant women at high risk of transmitting HBV to their infants due to high HBV DNA levels (≥200,000 IU/mL) or positive HBeAg status. This prophylaxis should begin preferably at the 28th week of pregnancy and continue until at least delivery, in addition to providing timely hepatitis B birth dose vaccination for all infants. However, significant challenges remain in accessing HBV DNA viral load or HBeAg serology testing, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. No studies have yet examined the clinical impact and feasibility of expanding antiviral prophylaxis access to all HBsAg-positive pregnant women. WHO commissioned a modeling study to explore different eligibility scenarios for antiviral prophylaxis. Modeling Studies: Scaling up HepB3 vaccination worldwide to 90% coverage, including a hepatitis B birth dose, could prevent an additional 14 million neonatal hepatitis B cases and 38,500 disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) over the next decade. A modeling study across 110 countries assessed the impact and cost-effectiveness of universal TDF prophylaxis for all HBsAg-positive pregnant women, regardless of HBV DNA levels, in settings without access to HBV DNA testing. This strategy could prevent 5 million new neonatal HBV infections and 2,969 DALYs from 2024 to 2030, with the highest impact in the WHO African Region. Overall, this approach could achieve a >90% reduction in new HBV infections globally between 2015 and 2030. Cost-Effectiveness: Prophylaxis for HBsAg-positive pregnant women with high HBV DNA levels or positive HBeAg status is likely cost-effective in only 26% of 106 countries analyzed, including China, South Africa, and Vietnam. Lower diagnostic and monitoring costs would make the strategy cost-effective in 70% of countries. Universal prophylaxis for all HBsAg-positive pregnant women would likely be cost-effective in 40% of countries. The relative cost-effectiveness of universal versus HBV DNA-driven strategies depends on the costs of treatment and diagnostic tests. Existing Recommendations: Where HBV DNA or HBeAg assays are available, there is strong evidence supporting TDF prophylaxis for HBsAg-positive pregnant women with HBV DNA levels ≥200,000 IU/mL or positive HBeAg status. This intervention is now a universal standard in settings with access to HBV DNA testing. Most clinical trials supporting this recommendation evaluated maternal TDF prophylaxis alongside infant HepB3 immunization and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) administration. Recent studies have demonstrated the efficacy of immunoglobulin-free strategies based on maternal TDF prophylaxis and timely infant birth-dose vaccination. Universal Prophylaxis: In settings without access to HBV DNA or HBeAg testing, universal TDF prophylaxis could reduce the risk of MTCT of HBV infection alongside HepB3 and birth-dose immunization. However, no studies have directly compared the effectiveness of universal versus targeted prophylaxis. Lowand middle-income countries with high HBsAg prevalence among pregnant women often overlap with those with low uptake of hepatitis B birth-dose vaccination. The WHO Guidelines Development Group recognized the lack of direct empirical evidence for universal prophylaxis but based its conditional recommendation on pragmatic considerations, including the significant balance of benefits versus harms and cost-effectiveness modeling data. Key Considerations: 1. Perinatal transmission remains the dominant mode of HBV transmission globally, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, where hepatitis B birth-dose vaccination uptake is low. Data indicate a significant residual risk (>10%) of MTCT among highly viremic pregnant women despite timely birth-dose vaccination. 2. Perinatal transmission is associated with a >90% risk of developing chronic hepatitis B (CHB), leading to liver complications such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). HBIG is not routinely available in most endemic countries and does not fully prevent MTCT among highly viremic women. 3. Reliable alternatives to HBV DNA testing, such as HBeAg rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), are lacking. Benefits of Universal Prophylaxis: 1. TDF is widely available at low cost globally, and dual therapy (TDF + 3TC or FTC) used in HIV ART programs may be more accessible in some countries. 2. Prophylaxis based on a positive HBsAg test alone could be easier to integrate and scale up in antenatal services in lowand middle-income countries with limited access to HBV DNA assays, reducing the time from HBsAg testing to initiating antiviral prophylaxis. 3. Universal prophylaxis enhances equity in settings with limited diagnostic capacity and provides an option to continue TDF for mothers meeting criteria for antiviral therapy for their own health. 4. Universal prophylaxis may compensate for suboptimal uptake and adherence to infant HBV vaccination, particularly timely birth-dose administration, in highly endemic regions. 5. Birth-dose vaccination alone may not provide complete protection without antiviral prophylaxis due to incomplete cross-genotype protection conferred by recombinant A2 HBV vaccines in some regions. 6. Expanding TDF use will also reduce horizontal transmission of HBV. Challenges and Harms: 1. Most HBsAg-positive pregnant women do not have HBV DNA levels ≥200,000 IU/mL and are not at risk of transmitting HBV to their offspring. Universal prophylaxis would result in unnecessary treatment for many women. 2. Expanded prophylaxis could lead to a misconception that peripartum TDF prophylaxis could replace timely hepatitis B birth-dose vaccination, which remains the most cost-effective option. 3. Mothers face potential risks of postpartum flare or exacerbation after discontinuing antiviral therapy, necessitating careful postpartum monitoring. 4. Universal prophylaxis will substantially increase demand for antiviral therapy, requiring sufficient procurement and a sustained supply chain, which could strain antenatal services in resource-limited settings. 5. Data on adherence to prophylaxis and its effectiveness in preventing MTCT are insufficient, and the optimal timing and duration of prophylaxis remain uncertain. Acceptability and Preferences: Studies indicate that most pregnant women (66–97%) prefer to receive TDF prophylaxis during pregnancy when needed and for their infants to receive a timely hepatitis B birth dose. However, preferences vary by region, with cost, affordability, accessibility, and safety being key determinants. Health-care workers have expressed concerns about the costs of prophylaxis, particularly in resource-limited settings where drug costs are paid out-of-pocket.
